question: Does the special rule for children of divorced or separated parents, or parents who lived apart (including parents who never married), apply to this person, for example because a Form 8332 release or a decree lets the noncustodial parent claim the child?

findings.situation: A custodial parent who signed Form 8332 for the year cannot tell whether the special rule 'applies to this person' when the filer is the parent giving the release rather than the parent using it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "If conditions (1) through (4) apply, only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents ... The custodial parent or another taxpayer, if eligible, can claim the child for the earned income credit and these other benefits."
findings.why: The question's example is framed around the noncustodial parent claiming. The rule still applies to the custodial parent's child and takes away that parent's CTC/ODC claim, so the custodial parent could reasonably answer either way.

findings.situation: A divorced or never-married custodial parent whose child lived with them more than half the year, with no Form 8332 or decree release, answers YES because the parents are divorced or lived apart.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent (defined later) if all of the following conditions apply."
findings.why: The question names 'children of divorced or separated parents, or parents who lived apart (including parents who never married)', which invites YES from any such parent. The rule only applies when all four conditions are met, and the tool computes this ordinary custodial case correctly from residency.

findings.situation: A noncustodial parent holds a signed Form 8332, but the child got over half of their support from someone other than the parents, or was not in either parent's custody for more than half the year, and the filer answers YES because of the release.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "2. The child received over half of the child's support for 2025 from the parents ... 3. The child is in custody of one or both of the parents for more than half of 2025."
findings.why: The question's example ('because a Form 8332 release ... lets the noncustodial parent claim the child') suggests the release alone triggers the rule. Here the rule does not apply, and the tool would correctly compute that the child is not a qualifying child because of the residency test.

locators: p. 17, Step 1, "Do you have a child who meets the conditions to be your qualifying child?"
p. 19, Step 4, "But see Children of divorced or separated parents"
p. 20, Children of divorced or separated parents
p. 21, Qualifying child of more than one person

question: Was this person married at the end of 2025, or is this person filing a joint return for 2025 (for example with a spouse who died during 2025)?

findings.situation: The dependent is married and files a separate return, or files a joint return only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax. The filer answers YES, but Steps 1 and 4 come out the same as for an unmarried person, and the tool already computes Step 1's joint-return condition.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Was this person married at the end of 2025...?" vs i1040gi p. 21, Married person: "if the person is married but doesn't file a joint return or files a joint return only to claim a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid, you may be able to claim that person as a dependent... In that case, go to Step 2, question 3 (for a qualifying child), or Step 4, question 4 (for a qualifying relative)."
findings.why: Marriage is not one of the Step 1 or Step 4 conditions; the IRS text sends a married non-joint filer back into the same flow. The qualifying_child and qualifying_relative lines are computed correctly for this person but are refused anyway.

findings.situation: The dependent's spouse died during 2025 and the dependent is not filing a joint return. The filer may answer NO (the person was widowed, not married, at year end) or YES (tax law treats the person as married for the year).
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 44, Married child: "A child who was married at the end of 2025 is a qualifying child only if (a) you can claim the child as your dependent, or (b)..."
findings.why: The question's example ties a spouse's death only to filing jointly, which suggests NO. If the child counts as married at year end, the eic_child line skips the dependency requirement and could wrongly come out true.

findings.situation: The dependent is legally separated under a decree of separate maintenance at the end of 2025. The filer may answer YES (still legally married) or NO (separated).
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 44, Married child: "A child who was married at the end of 2025..."
findings.why: The question does not say whether a legally separated person counts as married. Reading it one way could wrongly refuse the EIC line, and reading it the other way could wrongly compute it.

question: Did you and others together provide over half of this person's support for 2025, with no one person providing over half (a multiple support situation), whoever claims the person?

findings.situation: The filer contributed to a multiple-support person, but another contributor claims the person, so the filer is not treated as providing over half and the tool's false result is correct, yet the question still requires YES.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'with no one person providing over half (a multiple support situation), whoever claims the person?' IRS i1040gi p. 21, Multiple support agreements: 'special rules may apply that would treat you as having provided over half of the support.'
findings.why: The tool correctly computes this case as not the filer's qualifying relative, because the filer did not provide over half and the special rule does not treat them as having done so. The words 'whoever claims the person' still force YES, so the tool refuses even though the refusal targets only 'A person claimed under a multiple support agreement.'

findings.situation: A filer could read 'whoever claims the person' as asking whether they themselves claim the person, or as telling them to answer regardless of who claims.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 21: 'If no one person contributed over half of the support of your relative ... but you and another person(s) provided more than half of your relative's support, special rules may apply'
findings.why: The trailing phrase has no clear grammatical role. Filers in the same situation could answer differently depending on whether they intend to claim the person under the agreement.

question: Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025, under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)?

findings.situation: A custodial parent has released the claim on Form 8332 (or under a qualifying decree) to a noncustodial parent the child did not live with. That custodial parent could truthfully answer NO, because the child does not meet the residency condition for the other parent, so the tool computes the child as the custodial parent's qualifying child.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 20: "A child will be treated as the qualifying child or qualifying relative of the child's noncustodial parent ... if all of the following conditions apply ... only the noncustodial parent can claim the child for purposes of the child tax credit and credit for other dependents"; p. 21: "...unless the special rule for Children of divorced or separated parents, described earlier, applies."
findings.why: The question asks whether the child meets the conditions to be another person's qualifying child. The IRS rule says the child is treated as the noncustodial parent's qualifying child even though the conditions are not met. The wording misses this case, and the custodial parent ends up computed as eligible for CTC/ODC purposes.

findings.situation: The filer is the child's only parent among the people who can claim the child (for example, a grandparent in the same household also qualifies) and the filer claims the child. The filer must answer YES even though the tie-breaker always gives the child to the filer, which matches what the tool computes.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 21 (and p. 44): "If only one of the persons is the child's parent, the child is treated as the qualifying child of the parent."
findings.question: Does this person meet the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person for 2025, under the dependent rules or under the EIC rules (which have no support test)?
findings.why: The question triggers on any competing person. When the filer is the sole parent and claims the child, the tie-breaker result equals the tool's computed result (qualifying child = true), so refusing this case is unnecessary.

findings.situation: A filer may not know whether the 'conditions' for another person include that person's own tests, such as the child being younger than that person, the child living with that person in the United States, or that person being required to file or filing only for a refund.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 17: "If the child meets the conditions to be a qualifying child of any other person (other than your spouse if filing jointly) for 2025, see Qualifying child of more than one person"; p. 21: "If you and any other person can claim the child as a qualifying child, the following rules apply."
findings.why: The IRS rule turns on whether another person 'can claim' the child. The question asks only whether the child 'meets the conditions.' A filer could reasonably answer either way when the other person has no filing requirement or would not or could not claim the child.

question: Elect an alternative allocation of Form 4952 line 4g to qualified dividends instead of capital gains first?

findings.situation: A filer has a carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024 but uses the default allocation, so they truthfully answer NO, and the tool sets line 2 to zero.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p.1: "2 Disallowed investment interest expense from 2024 Form 4952, line 7"; p.3: "You don't have any carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024."
findings.why: The question asks only about the line 4g allocation election. It says nothing about a prior-year carryover, so the filer answers NO and the carryover is dropped. Dropping it understates line 3 and the deduction, and it also misstates the filing-exception test.

findings.situation: A filer has deductible investment expenses other than interest, such as depreciation or depletion on investment assets or expenses reported on a K-1. They answer NO, and the tool sets line 5 to zero.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p.4, Line 5: "Investment expenses are your allowed deductions, other than interest expense, directly connected with the production of investment income. For example, depreciation or depletion allowed on assets that produce investment income is an investment expense."
findings.why: Nothing in a question about allocating line 4g prompts a YES for line 5 expenses. Treating them as zero overstates net investment income and the allowed deduction, and it also wrongly applies the filing exception, which requires "You don't have any other deductible investment expenses."

findings.situation: A filer elects a line 4g amount when line 4e is zero, so the whole amount comes from qualified dividends under the default rule. They may read the question as asking whether they are electing to include qualified dividends, and answer YES.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p.4: "The amount on line 4g is generally treated as being attributable first to net capital gain from property held for investment (line 4e), and then to qualified dividends (line 4b)."
findings.why: The wording "allocation of Form 4952 line 4g to qualified dividends instead of capital gains first" does not clearly separate the ordinary line 4g election, which the tool supports, from the "Elec." reallocation on the line 4e dotted line. A filer whose election lands on qualified dividends anyway may answer YES and be refused, even though the tool would compute their return correctly.

question: Any prior-year disallowed investment interest carryover?

findings.situation: A filer has no carryover but does have other deductible investment expenses, such as depreciation or depletion on investment assets or K-1 investment expenses, so they answer NO and line 5 is computed as zero.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 4, Line 5: "Investment expenses are your allowed deductions, other than interest expense, directly connected with the production of investment income. For example, depreciation or depletion allowed on assets that produce investment income is an investment expense. Include investment expenses incurred directly by you or reported to you on Schedule K-1..."
findings.why: Line 5 and the filing-exception test in the `required` helper depend on these expenses, but the question asks only about a prior-year carryover. A filer with investment expenses and no carryover truthfully answers NO, and the tool treats line 5 as zero, which overstates net investment income and can wrongly apply the filing exception (p. 3: "You don't have any other deductible investment expenses").

findings.situation: A filer had disallowed investment interest in an earlier year that was fully used by 2024, so their 2024 Form 4952 line 7 is zero, but they may still answer YES because they once had a carryover.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p. 1, line 2: "Disallowed investment interest expense from 2024 Form 4952, line 7"; p. 3: "You don't have any carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024."
findings.why: "Any prior-year disallowed investment interest carryover" does not tie the answer to the amount on 2024 Form 4952 line 7. A filer could read it as any past carryover, even one already used up, and the tool would refuse a case it computes correctly.

question: Any interest expense attributable to royalties, a business, passive activities, tax-exempt income or at-risk limitations; any deductible investment expense other than interest (for example depreciation or depletion on assets that produce investment income, or investment expenses on a Schedule K-1); or any other investment income or expense beyond interest, dividends and securities sales?

findings.situation: A filer whose only items are securities interest and dividends but who has disallowed investment interest carried forward from 2024 Form 4952, line 7, can truthfully answer NO, and line 2 is then set to zero.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p.1, line 2: "Disallowed investment interest expense from 2024 Form 4952, line 7"; p.3, Exception: "You don't have any carryover of disallowed investment interest expense from 2024."
findings.why: The question never asks about a prior-year carryover. A carryover is still interest, so it is not "beyond interest, dividends and securities sales." The tool would drop a real line 2 amount and could wrongly apply the filing exception.

findings.situation: A filer with margin interest on securities who also pays interest on an unrelated business loan, or on a passive rental loan, must answer YES, although that interest is never part of Form 4952.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Any interest expense attributable to royalties, a business, passive activities..."; f4952 p.3: "Investment interest expense doesn't include ... Interest expense that is properly allocable to a passive activity."
findings.why: The wording covers any business or passive interest the filer has. It is not limited to investment interest that has to be split under the p.4 line 8 instructions, so the question refuses filers whose Form 4952 the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer whose Schedule K-1 reports investment expenses that are miscellaneous itemized deductions, or that are used in figuring passive income or loss, may answer YES because of the K-1 example, or NO because the expenses aren't deductible.
findings.irs_text: f4952 p.4, line 5: "Investment expenses don't include any deductions used in determining your income or loss from a passive activity. Don't include any miscellaneous itemized deductions..."
findings.why: The question's example "investment expenses on a Schedule K-1" conflicts with its own qualifier "deductible." A filer can't tell whether nondeductible K-1 expenses call for a YES answer.

question: Any of these: HSA distributions in 2025 that were not all used for qualified medical expenses or rolled over to another HSA; a qualified HSA funding distribution from an IRA in 2025; contributions by you or your employer to an Archer MSA for 2025 (Form 8853); excess HSA contributions from an earlier year; failing to remain an eligible individual during a testing period that began in an earlier year (last-month rule or qualified HSA funding distribution); or an HSA you acquired because of the account beneficiary's death?

findings.situation: A filer whose only YES item is a 2025 HSA distribution not used for medical expenses or rolled over, a failed testing period that began in an earlier year, or an inherited HSA answers YES, so line 13 is refused. Yet none of these enters lines 2 through 12, and the tool's 'smaller of line 2 or line 12' would still be correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'HSA distributions in 2025 that were not all used for qualified medical expenses or rolled over ...; failing to remain an eligible individual during a testing period that began in an earlier year ...; or an HSA you acquired because of the account beneficiary's death?' — f8889 (2025) p.1: '13 HSA deduction ... Subtract line 11 from line 8'; '16 Taxable HSA distributions ... Schedule 1 (Form 1040), Part I, line 8f'; '18 Last-month rule ... 20 Total income'
findings.why: On the form, these situations feed only Part II (lines 14a–17b) and Part III (lines 18–21). They never reach line 13, whose inputs are line 2 and lines 3–12, so line 13 is refused in cases the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer who made excess HSA contributions in an earlier year but withdrew them, with earnings, by that year's return due date cannot tell whether they have 'excess HSA contributions from an earlier year'.
findings.irs_text: i8889 (2025) p.7, Line 10: 'See the discussions under Line 13 for the treatment of excess contributions.' f8889 (2025) p.1, line 14b: 'any excess contributions ... that were withdrawn by the due date of your return'
findings.why: The question does not say whether excess contributions that were corrected count, or only excess still in the account that could be deducted or taxed this year. Filers could reasonably answer either way.

question: Any self-employment income (including church employee income), RRTA compensation, tips not reported to your employer or allocated tips in Form W-2 box 8 (Form 4137), Form 8919 wages, uncollected Medicare tax in Form W-2 box 12 (codes B or N), or Medicare wages on a wage statement from a U.S. territory (such as Form 499R-2/W-2PR)?

findings.situation: A filer whose only self-employment activity produced a net loss would truthfully answer YES to 'Any self-employment income', but the tool already enters zero on line 8, which is the correct amount.
findings.irs_text: f8959 (2025) p.1 line 8: 'Self-employment income from Schedule SE (Form 1040), Part I, line 6. If you had a loss, enter -0-'; i8959 (2025) p.1: 'A self-employment loss shouldn't be considered for purposes of this tax.'
findings.why: The screen refuses filers whose line 8 must be zero. The tool's zero is correct for them, so 'self-employment income' is broader than the positive Schedule SE line 6 amount the line needs.

findings.situation: A filer with a Form W-2GU, W-2AS, W-2CM or W-2VI must answer YES to 'Medicare wages on a wage statement from a U.S. territory', even though those forms report Medicare wages and tax in boxes 5 and 6 like Form W-2, so the tool's box 5 and box 6 totals compute lines 1 and 19 correctly.
findings.irs_text: i8959 (2025) p.1: 'References to Form W-2 on Form 8959 and in these instructions also apply to Forms W-2AS, W-2CM, W-2GU, W-2VI, and 499R-2/W-2PR. However, for Form 499R-2/W-2PR, Medicare wages and tips are reported in box 22 and Medicare tax withheld is reported in box 23.'
findings.why: Only Form 499R-2/W-2PR uses different boxes. The question's 'U.S. territory (such as Form 499R-2/W-2PR)' covers every territory form, including ones the box 5 and box 6 path handles.

question: Any recovery or refund in 2025 of an amount deducted on an earlier Form 8960 (for example a state or local income tax refund, or a refund of foreign income tax), even if none of it is taxable on Form 1040?

findings.situation: In 2025 the filer recovers an amount deducted in a post-2012 year when they filed no Form 8960 because MAGI was below the threshold, but that year produced an NOL part of which is a section 1411 NOL; the tool would leave line 7 at zero.
findings.irs_text: i8960 (2025) p. 15, Deduction Recoveries Worksheet line 1: "Don't include recoveries of items if the amount relates to a deduction taken in a tax year beginning after 2012, and you weren't subject to the NIIT solely because your MAGI was below the applicable threshold. This rule doesn't apply if you incurred an NOL in such year, and a portion of such NOL constitutes a section 1411 NOL." The worksheet then uses lines 14–16, "Calculation of recoveries when the deduction is taken into account in computing your section 1411 NOL."
findings.why: The recovery still has to go on line 7 through the section 1411 NOL recomputation, but the filer never filed a Form 8960 for that year. A filer could truthfully say NO to a refund 'of an amount deducted on an earlier Form 8960.'

findings.situation: The filer filed a prior-year Form 8960 anyway, deducting state income tax on line 9b, in a year when MAGI was below the threshold and there was no NOL; the 2025 refund of that tax adds nothing to line 7, which the tool computes as zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Any recovery or refund in 2025 of an amount deducted on an earlier Form 8960 ... even if none of it is taxable on Form 1040?" i8960 (2025) p. 15: "If the recovered amount relates to a deduction taken in a tax year beginning after 2012 and you weren't subject to the NIIT because your MAGI ... was below the applicable threshold on line 14, then [none is included]."
findings.why: The wording makes this filer answer YES and be refused, although the IRS text excludes the recovery entirely and the tool's zero on line 7 is correct.

findings.situation: A filer receives a 2025 state income tax refund for a year when the tax was deducted on Schedule A and only an allocated portion appeared on Form 8960 line 9b.
findings.irs_text: i8960 (2025) p. 15, worksheet line 4: "Enter the percentage of the deduction allocated to NII in the prior year." Also line 5: "the total amount deducted on the prior-year Form 8960 attributable to items recovered."
findings.why: A filer may see the refund as a refund of the Schedule A deduction rather than of 'an amount deducted on an earlier Form 8960.' A filer may also not know whether the allocated portion counts, so the same facts could be answered either way.

locators: p. 22, line 13; absent section 911/CFC/PFIC adjustments MAGI equals AGI
pp. 14–15, deduction recoveries; compare state/local income tax refund worksheet

question: Does this group need an appraisal or other special treatment: a deduction over $5,000, before any income limit, for one item or for similar items given to all donees together (other than publicly traded securities), a noncash contribution reaching you through a Schedule K-1, vehicles, pass-through entity interests, intellectual property, inventory, conservation or partial interests, property with restrictions on its use, or a clothing or household item over $500 not in good used condition?

findings.situation: A filer gives property worth more than $5,000, but the required reductions (for example, ordinary income property cut back to basis) bring the deduction to $5,000 or less, so they truthfully answer NO even though the instructions say a qualified appraisal is needed for any gift valued over $5,000.
findings.irs_text: "A separate, qualified appraisal is required for any gift of property valued in excess of $5,000." (i8283 Rev. 12-2025, p. 3, Section B)
findings.why: The question asks only about a deduction over $5,000. It never mentions a value over $5,000, so a gift that needs an appraisal under this sentence can slip past the screen and be computed with no appraisal.

findings.situation: A filer whose property is worth more than $5,000 but whose deduction drops below $5,000 after the required reductions cannot tell which amount the $5,000 test uses.
findings.irs_text: "'amount of your deduction' means your deduction before applying any income limits... Make any required reductions to the amount of the contributions before you determine if you must file Form 8283." (i8283 Rev. 12-2025, p. 1, Who Must File)
findings.why: The question says "a deduction over $5,000, before any income limit" but does not say whether to apply the valuation or basis reductions first. A filer could test either the full fair market value or the reduced amount.

findings.situation: A filer who gives more than $5,000 of securities that are not publicly traded but meet the Regulations 1.170A-13(c)(7)(xi)(B) exception answers YES, even though these go in Section A, need no appraisal, and the tool would compute them.
findings.irs_text: "The following items even if the claimed value was more than $5,000... d. Certain other securities even though the securities do not meet any of the criteria described in paragraphs 2.a through 2.c above" (i8283 Rev. 12-2025, p. 3, Section A)
findings.why: The question exempts only "publicly traded securities" from the over-$5,000 test. That forces a YES for the other securities that the instructions also place in Section A.

findings.situation: A filer with one piece of clothing or household item in poor condition cannot tell whether "over $500" means its value or the deduction claimed for it.
findings.irs_text: "a single article of clothing or household item that is not in good used condition or better and for which you are claiming a deduction of over $500" (i8283 Rev. 12-2025, p. 3, Section B)
findings.why: The question says "a clothing or household item over $500" and does not say over $500 of what. A filer could compare the item's value or the deduction to $500 and get different answers.

locators: pp. 1–3, Who Must File and Which Sections To Complete; f8283 Section A

question: Do any wage statements report railroad retirement compensation or taxes (W-2 box 14), or did you file Form CT-2 as an employee representative?

findings.situation: A single filer with one railroad employer reports RRTA compensation of $200,000 or less in W-2 box 14 (with no other employer and no CT-2). The question makes them answer YES, but the tool's no-path results are already correct: excess-tax credit zero, box 5 and box 6 totals unchanged, and Form 8959 Part III and line 23 both zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'Do any wage statements report railroad retirement compensation or taxes (W-2 box 14)…?' i1040gi p. 117, Sch. 3 line 11: 'If you … had more than one employer for 2025 and total wages of more than $176,100, too much social security or tier 1 railroad retirement (RRTA) tax may have been withheld… But if any one employer withheld more than $10,918.20, you can't claim the excess on your return.' iw2w3 p. 13: boxes 3–7 'are not to be used to report railroad retirement compensation and taxes.' i8959 p. 1: 'RRTA compensation should be separately compared to the threshold' ($200,000 single); p. 2: 'A railroad employer must withhold Additional Medicare Tax on compensation it pays to you in excess of $200,000.'
findings.why: RRTA amounts never appear in W-2 boxes 5 or 6, so the box 5 and box 6 totals are correct for these filers. With one employer there is no Schedule 3 line 11 credit, and with RRTA compensation at or below $200,000 Form 8959 lines 16, 17 and 23 are all zero. Answering YES on any box 14 RRTA amount therefore refuses returns the tool would compute correctly.

locators: pp. 12–13, Railroad employers: RRTA compensation and taxes in box 14; boxes 3–7 are not used for RRTA

question: Do you have any of these: qualified business income or loss, or PTP income or loss, other than section 199A dividends; a prior-year qualified business, REIT or PTP loss carryforward (including suspended losses allowed this year); or are you a patron in a specified agricultural or horticultural cooperative (including any qualified payments from one on Form 1099-PATR)?

findings.situation: A filer is a patron of an agricultural or horticultural cooperative that is not a 'specified' cooperative, or does not know whether it is one, and has only section 199A dividends otherwise.
findings.irs_text: f8995 (2025) p.1: "Use this form if your taxable income ... is at or below $197,300 ... and you aren't a patron of an agricultural or horticultural cooperative."
findings.why: Form 8995 shuts out any patron of an agricultural or horticultural cooperative, but the question asks only about a 'specified' cooperative. Such a filer can truthfully answer NO, and the tool then computes Form 8995 amounts the form says this filer may not use.

findings.situation: A filer has a business or PTP loss on a Schedule K-1 that is fully suspended this year (for example by the section 469 passive-loss rules or the section 465 at-risk rules) and has no other QBI items.
findings.irs_text: i8995 (2025) p.3: "Losses or deductions from a qualified trade or business that are suspended by other provisions of the Internal Revenue Code are not qualified losses or deductions and, therefore, are not included in your QBI for the year."
findings.why: The question's "qualified business income or loss, or PTP income or loss" can be read to include a loss that was incurred but suspended, which pushes the filer to YES. Under the IRS text that loss is not QBI this year, so a computed zero is correct, which would make this a WIDE case. Read the other way, the filer answers NO.

question: Does this distribution involve any of these: an early distribution with no known exception (code 1, J or S); a disability pension received before minimum retirement age, or a pension partly excludable because you were disabled as a result of a terrorist attack; a corrective distribution of excess deferrals or contributions; a qualified charitable distribution or HSA funding distribution; nondeductible contributions to any traditional IRA; a conversion, recharacterization or returned contribution (Form 8606); a rollover to a Roth IRA or designated Roth account; a lump-sum distribution you may report on Form 4972; a nonqualified annuity; the retired public safety officer premium exclusion; a death benefit exclusion; a plan loan offset; a Form RRB-1099-R; U.S. Civil Service retirement benefits under the alternative annuity option (Pub. 721); or a pension or annuity in which you have after-tax cost whose annuity starting date was before November 19, 1996, or for which the Simplified Method does not apply (the General Rule)?

findings.situation: A filer takes a nonqualified Roth IRA distribution coded T and made their first Roth IRA contribution in 2021 or later, without rolling it over. Nothing in the question covers this, so the filer answers NO, and the tool treats the taxable amount as the part not rolled over instead of sending the filer to Form 8606.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "2. You received a distribution from a Roth IRA. But if either (a) or (b) below applies, enter -0- on line 4b ... a. Distribution code T is shown in box 7 of Form 1099-R and you made a contribution (including a conversion) to a Roth IRA for 2020 or an earlier year. b. Distribution code Q"
findings.why: The question names only nondeductible traditional IRA contributions, conversions, recharacterizations, returned contributions and early distributions coded J. An ordinary Roth IRA distribution that still needs Form 8606 (code T with contributions from 2021 or later) matches none of these items.

findings.situation: A filer receives a distribution from a designated Roth account in an employer plan that is not qualified (code B, not rolled over). Nothing in the question covers this, so the filer answers NO, and the tool runs the pension or Simplified Method path.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30, Rollovers: "See Pub. 575 for more details on rollovers, including special rules that apply to rollovers from designated Roth accounts"; p. 28: "If your Form 1099-R doesn't show the taxable amount, you must use the General Rule explained in Pub. 939"
findings.why: The question mentions designated Roth accounts only as a rollover destination. A distribution from one that isn't rolled over needs Pub. 575, but the filer would answer NO.

findings.situation: A filer receives a one-time, non-annuity distribution from an employer plan that includes after-tax contributions (box 5) and rolls over part of it. They may not think of this as a 'pension or annuity in which you have after-tax cost' with a Simplified Method question, so they may answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 30, Rollovers: "Enter on line 5a the distribution from Form 1099-R, box 1. From this amount, subtract any contributions (usually shown in box 5) that were taxable to you when made. From that result, subtract the amount of the rollover."
findings.why: The tool's taxable-pension helper applies only the Simplified Method to after-tax cost, and its rollover helper ignores box 5. The question frames after-tax cost only in terms of annuity starting dates and the Simplified Method, so a filer could reasonably read it either way for a lump-sum payment.

findings.situation: A filer had excess IRA contributions from an earlier year returned in 2025. Each excess contribution has its own exception in the IRS text, and the filer may not count it as a 'returned contribution (Form 8606)'.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 27, Exception 2: "4. You had a 2024 or 2025 IRA contribution returned to you ... 5. You made excess contributions to your IRA for an earlier year and had them returned to you in 2025."
findings.why: The question's single phrase 'returned contribution' may read as covering only the timely return in item 4, not earlier-year excess contributions returned in 2025 (item 5).

question: Did you make contributions in 2025 to a governmental unemployment compensation program (not counting paid family leave or disability insurance contributions), or repay in 2025 any unemployment compensation you included in income in an earlier year?

findings.situation: A filer receives unemployment compensation in 2025 and made contributions to a governmental unemployment compensation program in an earlier year (for example 2024 payroll withholding in a state that taxes employees), but made none in 2025.

findings.why: The question ('Did you make contributions in 2025 to a governmental unemployment compensation program...') makes this filer answer YES and the tool refuses. With no compensation received there is nothing to reduce, so the line is -0-, which the tool computes correctly.

question: Are you required to file Form 6251 or do you have an AMT adjustment requiring its review?

findings.situation: A filer who owes no AMT but must repay excess advance premium tax credit, or has another line 1a–1y addition to tax, answers NO, and the tool still sets line 3 to zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 2025 p.1: "3 Add lines 1z and 2. Enter here and on Form 1040, 1040-SR, or 1040-NR, line 17"; "1z Add lines 1a through 1y"
findings.why: Line 3 includes line 1z additions to tax that have nothing to do with Form 6251 or AMT, so the AMT-only question never brings them up and the zeroed line drops them.

findings.situation: A filer with self-employment tax (line 4) and no AMT answers NO, and the tool's line 21 adds only lines 11 and 12, so the SE tax is left out of total other taxes.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 2025 p.2: "21 Add lines 4, 7 through 16, 18, and 19. These are your total other taxes."; p.1: "4 Self-employment tax. Attach Schedule SE."
findings.why: Line 21 also needs line 4, line 7, lines 8–10, lines 13–16, line 18 and line 19, none of which relate to AMT, so the question does not reach them.

findings.situation: A filer with an additional 10% tax on an early IRA distribution (line 8), household employment taxes (line 9), or a line 17 item such as additional tax on HSA distributions (via line 18) answers NO, and line 21 omits these amounts.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 2025 p.1: "8 Additional tax on IRAs or other tax-favored accounts. Attach Form 5329"; "9 Household employment taxes. Attach Schedule H"; p.2: "18 Total additional taxes. Add lines 17a through 17z"
findings.why: The question asks only about Form 6251. A filer with any of these taxes truthfully answers NO, and the tool's line 21 treats them as zero.

findings.situation: A filer who must file Form 6251 but whose alternative minimum tax works out to zero (for example, because of AMT adjustments or a credit limitation) answers YES and is refused, even though the tool's zero on line 2 is correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file Form 6251 ..."; f1040s2 2025 p.1: "2 Alternative minimum tax. Attach Form 6251"
findings.why: Line 2 needs only the AMT amount, and that amount is zero here. Being required to file Form 6251 does not by itself mean line 2 is nonzero.

findings.situation: A filer cannot tell what counts as an "AMT adjustment requiring its review", such as an ISO exercise, state tax deduction, or depreciation difference that may or may not lead to any AMT.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or do you have an AMT adjustment requiring its review?"; f1040s2 2025 p.1: "2 Alternative minimum tax. Attach Form 6251"
findings.why: The phrase is undefined. One filer may answer YES for any AMT preference item, while another answers NO unless they know AMT is actually owed.

question: Any amount on Schedule 2 other than Additional Medicare Tax or Net Investment Income Tax, for example the alternative minimum tax, repayment of excess advance premium tax credit or of a clean vehicle credit, self-employment tax, household employment taxes, the additional tax on early retirement or HSA distributions (often called a penalty), uncollected social security or Medicare tax on tips or group-term life insurance (W-2 box 12 codes A, B, M or N), tax on unreported tips (Form 4137), or interest on deferred tax?

findings.situation: A filer whose only Schedule 2 entry is a section 965 net tax liability installment from Form 965-A must answer YES, but that amount is not part of line 21, line 3, or Schedule 8812 line 22, so the tool's computed lines would be correct.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 2025 p.2: "20 Section 965 net tax liability installment from Form 965-A" and "21 Add lines 4, 7 through 16, 18, and 19."
findings.why: The question asks about "Any amount on Schedule 2 other than Additional Medicare Tax or Net Investment Income Tax." Line 20 is an amount on Schedule 2, but no refused line includes it, so the tool computes those lines correctly even when line 20 has an amount.

findings.situation: A worker who owes uncollected social security and Medicare tax on wages via Form 8919 (e.g., misclassified as a contractor) might answer NO because the examples list only tip-related and W-2 box 12 items and Form 4137, not Form 8919.
findings.irs_text: f1040s2 2025 p.1: "6 Uncollected social security and Medicare tax on wages. Attach Form 8919"; f1040s8812 2025 p.2 line 22: "...Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 6..."
findings.why: The general wording "any amount on Schedule 2" does cover Form 8919. However, the filer is answering before Schedule 2 exists, and the long example list names the neighboring lines 5 and 13 while leaving out line 6. A filer could reasonably take the list as the full set of uncollected-tax items.

question: Did you receive any nontaxable combat pay in 2025 (it is generally shown in Form W-2, box 12, code Q)?

findings.situation: A filer received nontaxable combat pay but chooses not to include it in earned income for the EIC, and is not claiming the additional child tax credit, so the Schedule 8812 Earned Income Worksheet is never reached; the filer must answer YES, yet zero is the correct EIC Step 5 line 4 amount.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Did you receive any nontaxable combat pay in 2025...?" vs. i1040gi p. 42, Step 5, line 4: "Enter all of your nontaxable combat pay if you elect to include it in earned income"; p. 43: "You can elect to include this pay in your earned income when figuring the EIC."
findings.why: EIC line 4 is nonzero only if the filer makes the election. A filer who does not elect has a correct zero, which the tool computes. Receipt alone forces YES and refuses the line. Only s8812 EIW line 1b ("Enter the amount of any nontaxable combat pay received") depends on receipt regardless of any election, and that line applies only when the worksheet is used.

locators: p. 42, Step 5, worksheet line 4; p. 43, Combat pay, nontaxable

question: Were you a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025?

findings.situation: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico has line 20 equal to or more than line 17, either with three or more qualifying children (line 16b of $5,100 or more) or with fewer than three, so line 27 is simply line 17.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Were you a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025?" Schedule 8812 (2025) page 2, after line 20: "Yes. If line 20 is equal to or more than line 17, skip Part II-B and enter the amount from line 17 on line 27." Page 2, line 26: "Enter the larger of line 20 or line 25" and "enter the smaller of line 17 or line 26 on line 27."
findings.why: With three or more children, the form skips Part II-B regardless of residency. With fewer than three, the smaller of line 17 and the larger of lines 20 and 25 is still line 17 when line 20 covers it. The tool computes line 17 correctly in both cases, but the question has every Puerto Rico resident answer YES and get refused.

findings.situation: A bona fide resident of Puerto Rico whose line 16a or line 16b is zero cannot take the additional child tax credit, so line 27 is zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Were you a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico in 2025?" Schedule 8812 (2025) page 2, line 16a: "If zero, stop here; you cannot take the additional child tax credit." Line 16b: "If zero, stop here; you cannot claim the additional child tax credit."
findings.why: The form stops before the Puerto Rico branch, and the tool's computation gives zero through line 17. The question still makes this filer answer YES and be refused.

locators: Schedule 8812 (2025), after line 20, "If you are a bona fide resident of Puerto Rico, go to line 21"

question: Are any charitable deductions reduced by income limits, or carried over from a prior year? Determine under Publication 526 before answering.

findings.situation: A filer paid foreign income taxes, or generation-skipping tax on certain income distributions, and chooses to deduct them. They have no charitable limits or carryover, so they answer NO, and the tool sets line 6 to zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p.7, Line 6 Other Taxes: "Include on this line income taxes you paid to a foreign country and generation-skipping tax (GST) imposed on certain income distributions."
findings.why: The question only asks about charitable deductions. Nothing in its wording reaches other taxes, yet answering NO makes line 6 zero.

findings.situation: A filer paid home mortgage interest that wasn't reported on Form 1098, for example to the seller of the home. They answer NO because their charitable gifts aren't limited, and the tool sets line 8b to zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040sa (2025) p.1, line 8b: "Home mortgage interest not reported to you on Form 1098 ... If paid to the person from whom you bought the home, see instructions and show that person's name, identifying no., and address"
findings.why: Mortgage interest has nothing to do with charitable income limits or carryovers, so a truthful NO drops a deduction the form allows.

findings.situation: A filer paid deductible points that weren't reported on Form 1098. They answer NO, and the tool sets line 8c to zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040sa (2025) p.1, line 8c: "Points not reported to you on Form 1098. See instructions for special rules"
findings.why: The charitable-only wording gives the filer no reason to say YES, so the points are silently dropped.

findings.situation: A filer has a casualty or theft loss from a federally declared disaster, figured on Form 4684. They answer NO, and the tool sets line 15 to zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040sa (2025) p.1, line 15: "Casualty and theft loss(es) from a federally declared disaster (other than net qualified disaster losses). Attach Form 4684 and enter the amount from line 18 of that form."
findings.why: Disaster losses are outside the question's charitable subject, so a truthful NO zeroes a line the IRS requires.

findings.situation: A filer owes federal estate tax on income in respect of a decedent, or has another deduction from the line 16 list. They answer NO, and the tool sets line 16 to zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sca (2025) p.7: "Don't include federal estate tax on income in respect of a decedent on this line; instead, include it on line 16."; f1040sa p.1, line 16: "Other—from list in instructions."
findings.why: The question never mentions other itemized deductions, but answering NO makes line 16 zero, and line 17 then understates the total.

findings.situation: A filer who hasn't worked through Publication 526 can't tell whether their gifts are "reduced by income limits," for example whether cash gifts plus noncash gifts exceed the AGI percentage limits.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are any charitable deductions reduced by income limits ... Determine under Publication 526 before answering."; f1040sa (2025) p.1, line 12: "Other than by cash or check. If you made any gift of $250 or more, see instructions."
findings.why: The answer depends on a calculation in a publication that isn't provided. A filer could read "reduced" as a limit they would have to apply themselves, or as one that has already taken effect, and so answer either way.

question: Can someone claim you or your spouse as a dependent for 2025, or are you a dual-status alien? (Answer no if the person who could claim you is not required to file and does not file, or files only to claim a refund of withheld or estimated tax.)

findings.situation: A single or head-of-household filer can be claimed as a dependent by a parent who has no filing requirement and files only to get back withheld tax. The question's parenthetical tells this filer to answer NO, so the tool gives the full standard deduction and never uses the Standard Deduction Worksheet for Dependents.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, line 12e: "Exception 1—Dependent. Line 12a. If you checked a box on line 12a, use the Standard Deduction Worksheet for Dependents to figure your standard deduction." i1040gi p. 35: "Use this worksheet only if someone can claim you, or your spouse if filing jointly, as a dependent."
findings.why: The refund-only exception comes from EIC Step 4 question 6 (i1040gi p. 42). The standard deduction text quoted here has no such exception. The tool uses one question with that exception for both lines, so for the standard deduction it can tell a filer to answer NO when the IRS text calls for the dependent worksheet, which limits the deduction to earned income plus $450 (minimum $1,350).

question: Does this sale involve collectibles (works of art, rugs, antiques, metals such as gold, silver or platinum bullion, gems, stamps, coins, alcoholic beverages or other tangible property of that kind), qualified small business stock with a section 1202 exclusion, depreciable real property (section 1250 property), or an interest in a partnership, S corporation or trust holding such property?

findings.situation: A filer sells stock in an S corporation, or an interest in a trust, that holds depreciable real property or QSB stock but no collectibles. The question's wording makes them answer YES, yet the gain is ordinary capital gain that the tool computes correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or an interest in a partnership, S corporation or trust holding such property". i1040sd p. 12, line 19 applies only if "You reported a long-term capital gain from the sale or exchange of an interest in a partnership that owned section 1250 property." i1040sd p. 11, line 18 looks through partnership, S corporation and trust interests only for gain "attributable to unrealized appreciation of collectibles."
findings.why: The IRS looks through an entity for section 1250 property only when the interest is in a partnership, and it never looks through for QSB stock. So an S corporation or trust interest holding only these assets, or a partnership interest holding only QSB stock, needs no line 18 or 19 worksheet.

findings.situation: A filer sells a partnership, S corporation or trust interest held 1 year or less, where the entity holds collectibles or section 1250 property. The question's wording makes them answer YES, yet no 28% or unrecaptured section 1250 gain arises.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 11, line 18: "any gain (but not loss) from the sale or exchange of an interest in a partnership, S corporation, or trust held for more than 1 year and attributable to unrealized appreciation of collectibles". i1040sd p. 12, line 19: "a long-term capital gain from the sale or exchange of an interest in a partnership that owned section 1250 property."
findings.why: The look-through rules apply only to interests held long-term. The question covers any interest holding such property no matter how long it was held, so it catches short-term sales of interests that the tool handles as ordinary sales.

findings.situation: A filer sells shares of a physically backed precious-metals fund (a grantor trust) reported on Form 1099-B as an ordinary security sale. They could reasonably think they sold shares, not a trust interest, and answer NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040sd p. 11: "Collectibles include ... metals (such as gold, silver, and platinum bullion) ..."; i1040sd p. 10: aggregate totals may be reported on line 1a or 8a "from any transactions (except sales of collectibles)"
findings.why: Strictly, the question covers this case through "a trust holding such property." But a filer holding exchange-traded shares could reasonably decide the sale doesn't "involve" bullion or a trust interest. The tool would then miss the collectibles gain and the code C entry.

locators: pp. 7–11, columns (e) through (h), codes B and W
Parts I and II, boxes G–L

question: Are you required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR)? Determine under its instructions; this tool does not determine foreign account values or exceptions.

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-INT that includes interest received as a nominee (or accrued interest paid on a bond purchase), has no foreign accounts, and so truthfully answers NO; the tool then puts the gross roster total on line 2 without the required subtraction.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.1: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total interest you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 2." p.2: "follow the rules earlier under Nominees ... identify the amount to be subtracted as 'Accrued Interest.'"
findings.why: Line 2 computes only the sum of interest.amount, but the IRS text requires subtracting nominee, accrued-interest, OID and ABP adjustments. FBAR status has nothing to do with these adjustments, so the screen never catches them.

findings.situation: A filer cashed post-1989 series EE or I bonds and paid qualified higher education expenses, has no foreign accounts, and so answers NO; line 3 is then forced to zero.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 3: "If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses ... you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815"
findings.why: Line 3 is hard-coded to zero, and the FBAR question gives a filer entitled to the Form 8815 exclusion no reason to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-DIV that includes ordinary dividends received as a nominee, has no foreign accounts, and so answers NO; line 6 then takes box 1a gross.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 5 Nominees: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total ordinary dividends you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 6."
findings.why: Line 6 copies box 1a with no nominee subtraction, and FBAR status does not bring this situation to light.

findings.situation: A filer who must file an FBAR (foreign accounts above $10,000 in aggregate) but has only ordinary Form 1099-INT/1099-DIV amounts with no adjustments answers YES, and lines 2, 3 and 6 are refused even though the tool would compute them correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR)?" i1040sb p.3: "A U.S. person that has a financial interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts must file the form if the aggregate value of foreign financial accounts exceeds $10,000"
findings.why: The FBAR requirement affects Part III (lines 7a/7b), not the interest and dividend amounts on lines 2, 3 and 6. A YES answer therefore blocks lines whose computation does not depend on it.

locators: pp. 1–3, interest, dividends and foreign accounts/trusts

question: Are you required to file Form 8938 for specified foreign financial assets?

findings.situation: A filer received a Form 1099-INT that includes interest received as a nominee, has no foreign assets, and so truthfully answers NO; the tool then puts the full interest on line 2 without subtracting the nominee distribution.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 1: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total interest you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 2."
findings.why: Line 2 is the line 1 subtotal less nominee amounts, but the tool only adds interest entries. The Form 8938 question has nothing to do with nominee status, so this filer is never screened out.

findings.situation: A filer must subtract accrued interest paid on a bond purchase, an OID adjustment, or an amortizable bond premium adjustment, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool reports gross interest on line 2.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "follow the rules earlier under Nominees to see how to report the accrued interest. But identify the amount to be subtracted as 'Accrued Interest.'" (similarly "OID Adjustment" and "ABP Adjustment")
findings.why: These subtractions reduce line 2 below the sum of interest entries. The tool does not make them, and a question about Form 8938 does not reach them.

findings.situation: A filer cashed post-1989 series EE or I savings bonds and paid qualified higher education expenses, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool sets line 3 to zero instead of the Form 8815 exclusion.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Line 3. If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses ... you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815"
findings.why: Line 3 is computed as a fixed zero, but the IRS text calls for a Form 8815 exclusion amount. Nothing in the Form 8938 question asks about savings bond redemptions or education expenses.

findings.situation: A filer received ordinary dividends as a nominee, answers NO because they have no foreign assets, and the tool enters the full Form 1099-DIV box 1a total on line 6.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total ordinary dividends you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 6."
findings.why: Line 6 must be reduced by nominee dividends, but the tool copies box 1a. The Form 8938 question does not identify nominee recipients.

findings.situation: A filer who is required to file Form 8938 must answer YES even though their interest and dividends are ordinary domestic amounts that the tool would put correctly on lines 2, 3 and 6.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are you required to file Form 8938 for specified foreign financial assets?"; i1040sb p. 2: "Regardless of whether you are required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR), you may be required to file Form 8938 ... with your income tax return."
findings.why: The Schedule B text treats Form 8938 only as a separate filing obligation. It does not change how lines 2, 3 or 6 are figured, so refusing these lines on a YES answer blocks amounts the tool computes correctly.

findings.situation: A filer with foreign accounts may not know whether they are "required" to file Form 8938, or may confuse that requirement with the FBAR or the line 7a foreign-account question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p. 2: "Regardless of whether you are required to file FinCEN Form 114 (FBAR), you may be required to file Form 8938" (no thresholds or definition of "specified foreign financial assets" are given)
findings.why: The Schedule B instructions do not give the Form 8938 thresholds or define "specified foreign financial assets." A filer with foreign accounts could reasonably answer either way.

locators: pp. 1–3, interest, dividends and foreign accounts/trusts

question: Received a distribution from, or were grantor of or transferor to, a foreign trust during 2025?

findings.situation: A filer who cashed post-1989 series EE or I savings bonds and paid qualified higher education expenses can exclude interest on line 3, but the tool forces line 3 to zero, and the filer truthfully answers NO to a foreign-trust question.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 3: "If, during 2025, you cashed series EE or I U.S. savings bonds issued after 1989 and you paid qualified higher education expenses ... you may be able to exclude part or all of the interest on those bonds. See Form 8815"
findings.why: The screen asks only about foreign trusts. Nothing in its wording reaches the Form 8815 exclusion, which the tool never computes.

findings.situation: A filer whose Form 1099-INT includes nominee interest, accrued interest paid on a bond purchase, an OID adjustment, or an ABP adjustment must subtract these to reach line 2, but the tool just adds interest amounts, and the filer answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.1, Nominees: "Below this subtotal, enter 'Nominee Distribution' ... Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 2." (also p.2, "Accrued Interest," "OID Adjustment," "ABP Adjustment")
findings.why: Line 2 is line 1 minus these subtractions, and the tool's plain sum ignores them. A foreign-trust question gives the filer no reason to answer YES.

findings.situation: A filer who received ordinary dividends as a nominee must subtract them to reach line 6, but the tool enters the full Form 1099-DIV box 1a total, and the filer answers NO.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.2, Line 5 Nominees: "enter 'Nominee Distribution' and show the total ordinary dividends you received as a nominee. Subtract this amount from the subtotal and enter the result on line 6."
findings.why: Box 1a includes the nominee amount, so the tool overstates line 6. The foreign-trust wording does not capture this case.

findings.situation: A filer with includible accrued market discount (including on a tax-exempt bond) or gain on a contingent payment debt instrument that is not shown as a reported interest entry answers NO, and the tool omits it from line 2.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.1, Line 1: "Also include any accrued market discount that is includible in income and any gain on a contingent payment debt instrument that is includible in income as interest income."
findings.why: These amounts belong in taxable interest even without a Form 1099 figure. Nothing in a foreign-trust question surfaces them.

findings.situation: A filer who received a foreign trust distribution but has only ordinary Form 1099-INT interest and Form 1099-DIV dividends with no adjustments answers YES, and the tool refuses lines 2, 3, and 6 even though its sums would be correct.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Received a distribution from, or were grantor of or transferor to, a foreign trust during 2025?"; i1040sb p.3, Line 8: "If you received a distribution from a foreign trust, you must provide additional information ... See the Instructions for Form 3520"
findings.why: The foreign-trust facts drive line 8 and Form 3520/3520-A, not the amounts on lines 2, 3, and 6. Those lines can be computed correctly anyway.

findings.situation: A filer who created or funded a foreign trust before 2025 that still existed in 2025, or who received only a loan of cash or securities from a foreign trust, could read the question either way.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb p.3, Line 8: "a loan of cash or marketable securities is generally considered to be a distribution"; "If you were the grantor of, or transferor to, a foreign trust that existed during 2025"
findings.why: Read naturally, "were grantor ... during 2025" means acting in 2025, and "distribution" suggests a non-loan payment. The IRS text covers both the earlier grantor and the loan.

question: Any nominee income, original issue discount reported in an amount other than on Form 1099-OID, accrued interest paid on a bond purchase, bond premium adjustment, accrued market discount, a contingent payment debt instrument, seller-financed mortgage interest, a savings bond interest exclusion, foreign corporation reporting, or other special treatment?

findings.situation: A filer who was an officer or director of a foreign corporation, or owned 10% or more of one, has a Form 5471 filing duty and answers YES to 'foreign corporation reporting', but that duty doesn't change the amounts on lines 2, 3 or 6, so the tool would compute them correctly.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'foreign corporation reporting'. i1040sb (2025) p. 2, Part II TIP: 'You may have to file Form 5471 if, in 2025, you were an officer or director of a foreign corporation... or owned 10% or more...' Line 5: 'Report on line 5 all of your ordinary dividends. This amount should be shown in box 1a of your Forms 1099-DIV'
findings.why: Form 5471 is a separate information return. It doesn't adjust Schedule B line 2, 3 or 6, so asking about it refuses returns the tool handles correctly.

findings.situation: A filer who received a Form 1099-OID and is reporting exactly the box 1 or box 8 amount may read 'reported in an amount other than on Form 1099-OID' as any OID not reported on a 1099-OID, or as OID reported at a different amount. A filer whose payer already netted acquisition premium may also not know which reading applies.
findings.irs_text: i1040sb (2025) p. 2: 'If you are reporting OID in an amount less than the amount shown in box 1 or box 8 of Form 1099-OID, follow the rules earlier under Nominees... identify the amount to be subtracted as "OID Adjustment."'
findings.why: The phrase can mean OID that came from somewhere other than a Form 1099-OID, or OID reported at an amount different from the form. The IRS rule only covers reporting less than box 1 or box 8.

findings.situation: A filer can't tell what counts as 'other special treatment'. For example, it's unclear whether tax-exempt interest, market discount on a tax-exempt bond, or a foreign account reported on line 7a would count.
findings.irs_text: Question: 'or other special treatment?' i1040sb (2025) p. 1: 'The market discount on a tax-exempt bond is taxable interest income and not tax-exempt interest.'
findings.why: The catch-all doesn't say what it includes. One filer could answer YES for items that don't affect lines 2, 3 or 6, while another answers NO for an item that does belong on line 1 and so in line 2.

question: Do you want to claim any credit other than the foreign tax credit claimed without Form 1116, the excess social security credit, the child tax credit, the credit for other dependents, the additional child tax credit and the earned income credit, or do you have any other amount for Schedule 3 Part I (for example a Form 8978 adjustment)?

findings.situation: A filer who had too much tier 1 railroad retirement (RRTA) tax withheld, but no excess social security tax, cannot tell whether that credit is one of the listed exceptions.
findings.irs_text: Schedule 3 (2025) line 11: 'Excess social security and tier 1 RRTA tax withheld'; i1040gi p. 117: 'too much social security or tier 1 railroad retirement (RRTA) tax may have been withheld. You can take a credit on this line'
findings.why: The question exempts only 'the excess social security credit', so a railroad worker could read the exception as excluding the RRTA part and answer YES. A YES fails scope.ready and refuses the whole return, even though the IRS treats both as one line 11 credit.

question: Any retirement, Social Security, nonresident alien (you or your spouse, for any part of 2025) or other income or return treatment outside wages, interest, dividends and supported securities sales, including wages or tips not on a Form W-2, Medicaid waiver payments (whether or not in Form W-2 box 1), dependent care or adoption benefits, other earned income (Form 1040 lines 1b-1h), or income or loss from a passive activity (including gain on selling an interest in one)?

findings.situation: A filer whose 2025 income is only W-2 wages and interest, but who has a net operating loss carryforward from an earlier year, could truthfully answer NO because the carryforward is not 2025 income; Form 1040 line 8 would still need it, and the tool would enter $0.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.1, line 8: "Additional income from Schedule 1, line 10"
findings.why: Schedule 1 line 10 is a net figure that can include negative items such as an NOL deduction. The question asks only about income received outside wages, interest and dividends, so a prior-year loss carried into 2025 does not plainly fall within it.

findings.situation: A filer whose only income is wages earned abroad, and who excludes them as foreign earned income, could answer NO because the income is wages; the exclusion still needs to be on Form 1040 line 8, and the tool would enter $0.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.1, line 8: "Additional income from Schedule 1, line 10"; i1040gi p.40, Step 1 q.3: "Are you filing Form 2555 (relating to foreign earned income)?"
findings.why: The question excludes wages from what it asks about. The foreign earned income exclusion reduces line 8 even though the underlying income is wages, and the question names neither the exclusion nor Form 2555.

findings.situation: A filer with an adjustment, an extra deduction or a credit (lines 10, 13b, 16, 19-20, 27-31 cited by the scope.ready refusal) but no unusual income cannot tell whether "other ... return treatment" includes their situation.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.1, line 10: "Adjustments to income from Schedule 1, line 26"; p.2, line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: The phrase "other income or return treatment outside wages, interest, dividends and supported securities sales" does not say which treatments count. One filer could read it as income items only and answer NO, while another could read it as any form or schedule and answer YES.

question: Any additional Form 1040 line 16 tax or filing, including filing Form 8814 (even with no tax), Form 4972, Form 8615, a section 962 election, Form 8621, a Form 8978 amount, or recapture of an education credit?

findings.situation: A filer has income or loss from a passive activity that never passes through Schedule 1, such as a capital gain from selling property used in a passive activity reported only on Form 1040 line 7a. The filer truthfully answers NO here and NO to the Schedule 1 screen, so the tool treats EIC Step 2 question 4 as 'No' and skips the Pub. 596 Worksheet 1 check.
findings.irs_text: 4. Do any of the following apply for 2025? ... • You are filing Form 8814 ... • You have income or loss from a passive activity. Yes. Use Worksheet 1 in Pub. 596 (i1040gi p. 40)
findings.why: eic.step2_other depends only on this line 16 screen and the Schedule 1 screen. Neither question asks about passive activity income or loss, and passive income does not always flow through Schedule 1.

findings.situation: A filer whose line 16 tax should be figured another way, such as by electing Schedule J farm income averaging, could fairly say they have no 'additional' line 16 tax or filing and answer NO. The tool would then compute the ordinary line 16 tax.
findings.irs_text: 16 Tax (see instructions). Check if any from Form(s): 1 8814 2 4972 3 ____ (f1040 2025 p. 2)
findings.why: The question names specific forms and then says 'any additional ... tax or filing'. It is ambiguous whether an alternative way of computing the tax, or another item entered at box 3 that the question does not name, counts as 'additional'.

(Schedule 1-A deductions are asked separately.)

findings.situation: A filer has a passive-activity gain that is not reported on Schedule E or a K-1 and is not self-employment income, such as an installment-sale gain this year from a former rental property reported through Form 6252/4797 or Schedule D.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 40, Step 2, question 4: "Do any of the following apply for 2025? ... • You have income or loss from a passive activity. Yes. Use Worksheet 1 in Pub. 596"
findings.why: The question lists only Schedule 1 items (Schedule E, K-1s, rental of personal property, Schedule C/F/SE). It never asks about passive activity income or loss in general, so this filer truthfully answers NO and eic.step2_other is computed as 'No'.

findings.situation: A filer owes uncollected social security and Medicare tax on tips or group-term life insurance (W-2 box 12 codes A/B/M/N), or tax on unreported tips (Form 4137) or Form 8919 wages, which go on Schedule 2, lines 13, 5 or 6.
findings.irs_text: f1040s8812 Schedule 8812 (2025), line 22: "Enter the total of the amounts from Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 15; Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 5; Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 6; and Schedule 2 (Form 1040), line 13"
findings.why: s8812.line22 is set to zero whenever this screen is answered NO, but the question asks only about Schedule 1 items. A filer with only these Schedule 2 amounts answers NO, and line 22 drops them unless an unlisted Schedule 2 screen catches them.

findings.situation: A filer received a small amount of wages from a church that elected exemption (under $108.28, so no Schedule SE is required), or is a minister with an approved Form 4361 who does not file Schedule SE.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 42, Step 5, question 1: "Are you filing Schedule SE because you were a member of the clergy or you had church employee income of $108.28 or more?"
findings.why: The question reads "Schedule SE (including clergy, and church employee income: wages from a church that elected exemption ...)". This can be read as asking about any clergy status or any church employee income, not only cases where Schedule SE is filed. Under that reading, a filer whose wages the tool handles correctly would answer YES.

question: Do you qualify for any Schedule 1-A deduction (qualified tips, qualified overtime compensation, qualified passenger vehicle loan interest, or the enhanced deduction for a filer born before January 2, 1961), whether or not you planned to claim it?

findings.situation: A filer born before January 2, 1961 has income high enough that the enhanced senior deduction phases out to zero, so Schedule 1-A line 38 is $0. The tool's $0 on line 13b would be correct, but the filer answers YES because of their birth date.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.2, line 12d: "You: Were born before January 2, 1961"; line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: The question names the deduction as "the enhanced deduction for a filer born before January 2, 1961," so birth date alone reads as qualifying. Any filer who checks the line 12d box would answer YES and be refused, even when the Schedule 1-A amount is zero. The income phase-out itself is not in the supplied text.

findings.situation: A filer received tips (line 1c or W-2) or overtime pay but does not know whether these count as "qualified tips" or "qualified overtime compensation."
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.1, line 1c: "Tip income not reported on line 1a (see instructions)"; p.2, line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: "Qualified" is a defined term that none of the supplied text explains, so a filer with tips or overtime could reasonably answer either way. If they answer NO when the items do qualify, line 13b becomes $0 and a deduction they are owed is missed.

findings.situation: A filer meets the basic conditions for a Schedule 1-A item (tips, overtime, vehicle loan interest, or age), but the computed deduction may be limited or reduced to zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p.2, line 13b: "Additional deductions from Schedule 1-A, line 38"
findings.why: "Qualify for any Schedule 1-A deduction, whether or not you planned to claim it" can mean meeting the eligibility conditions or having a nonzero amount. Filers whose amount works out to zero could answer either way.
