question: Is there a capital loss carried into 2025 from any earlier year?

findings.situation: A filer with a short-term or long-term capital gain or loss passed through on a partnership, S corporation, estate, or trust Schedule K-1, but no prior-year capital loss, truthfully answers NO, and lines 5 and 12 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 5 Net short-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 ... 12 Net long-term gain or (loss) from partnerships, S corporations, estates, and trusts from Schedule(s) K-1 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The question asks only about carryovers. Pass-through capital gain or loss is a separate source that the wording never mentions, so the tool treats it as zero without refusing.

findings.situation: A filer with an installment-sale gain (Form 6252), a casualty or theft gain or loss (Form 4684), a section 1256 or straddle result (Form 6781), a like-kind exchange (Form 8824), a Form 4797 Part I gain, or undistributed long-term gain (Form 2439) truthfully answers NO, and lines 4 and 11 are entered as zero.
findings.irs_text: 4 Short-term gain from Form 6252 and short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 ... 11 Gain from Form 4797, Part I; long-term gain from Forms 2439 and 6252; and long-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824 (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: None of these sources is a carryover from an earlier year, so a truthful NO zeroes lines 4 and 11. The line labels ('zero only after unsupported source/carryover screening') assume a source screen that this question does not perform.

findings.situation: A filer had a net capital loss on the 2024 Schedule D, or negative 2024 taxable income, but does not know whether any of the loss remains after the $3,000 deduction, so cannot tell whether a loss is 'carried into 2025'.
findings.irs_text: 6 Short-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 8 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet in the instructions ... 14 Long-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 13 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet (f1040sd 2025, p. 1)
findings.why: The carryover amount is the result of the worksheet, so 'is there a capital loss carried into 2025' can only be answered after the worksheet the tool declines to prepare. A filer whose prior loss may have been fully absorbed could reasonably answer either way.

question: Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797, 2439, 6252, 4684, 6781 or 8824, or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1 (for example section 1256 contracts or a casualty or theft of property)?

findings.situation: A filer who has a short-term or long-term capital loss carryover from the prior year, and no other listed source forms or K-1 items, truthfully answers NO, so lines 6 and 14 are treated as zero.
findings.irs_text: f1040sd (2025) p.1, line 6: "Short-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 8 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet"; line 14: "Long-term capital loss carryover. Enter the amount, if any, from line 13 of your Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet"
findings.why: The question names only Forms 4797, 2439, 6252, 4684, 6781, 8824 and K-1 capital items. A prior-year carryover is none of these, so nothing in the wording prompts a YES, yet lines 6 and 14 are among the lines this screen governs.

findings.situation: A filer whose only Form 4797 amounts are ordinary gains or losses (Part II or Part III recapture), or a Part I net section 1231 loss, answers YES even though none of it reaches Schedule D lines 4–14, which would correctly be zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "Are there gains or losses from (or that belong on) Forms 4797..."; f1040sd (2025) p.1, line 11: "Gain from Form 4797, Part I"
findings.why: Schedule D takes only the Part I gain from Form 4797. Ordinary 4797 amounts and 1231 losses go elsewhere, but the question's 'gains or losses from... 4797' wording forces a YES.

findings.situation: A filer with a personal-use casualty or theft whose Form 4684 losses exceed gains (the net loss goes to Schedule A), or whose casualty involves business property (it flows to Form 4797 ordinary), answers YES although Schedule D line 4/11 would correctly be zero.
findings.irs_text: Question: "...Forms ... 4684 ... (for example ... a casualty or theft of property)"; f1040sd (2025) p.1, line 4: "short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684"
findings.why: Only the 4684 amounts that are capital and net to a gain for personal-use property reach Schedule D. The question asks about any casualty or theft gain or loss.

findings.situation: A filer may be unsure whether section 1256 contracts or a casualty or theft are being asked about only when they come through a Schedule K-1, or whenever they occur.
findings.irs_text: Question: "or capital gains or losses on a Schedule K-1 (for example section 1256 contracts or a casualty or theft of property)"; f1040sd (2025) p.1, line 4: "short-term gain or (loss) from Forms 4684, 6781, and 8824"
findings.why: The examples are placed after the K-1 clause. A filer with a directly held 1256 contract or casualty, and no K-1, could read the parenthetical as limited to K-1 items. Forms 6781 and 4684 are named earlier in the question, but the placement invites misreading.

question: Are any of your benefits disability payments for injuries incurred as a direct result of a terrorist attack directed against the United States or its allies (including injuries covered by the September 11 Victim Compensation Fund)?

findings.situation: A filer was disabled in a terrorist attack, but in an earlier year reached full retirement age, so all of this year's SSA benefits are retirement benefits.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 31: "Because you became eligible for a full retirement benefit in May, the month after you turned age 66, you can exclude only 4 months (January through April) of your annual benefit from income ($6,000). You must report the remaining $12,000 on line 6a."
findings.why: The question doesn't say that benefits paid after full retirement age stop being disability payments. Such a filer could answer YES because the benefits trace back to the injury, even though nothing is excludable and the tool would compute the lines correctly.

findings.situation: A filer receives terrorist-attack disability payments from a source other than SSA or RRB, such as an employer or public-safety disability pension, and receives ordinary taxable social security benefits.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 32, line 1: "Enter the total amount from box 5 of all your Forms SSA-1099 and RRB-1099"; p. 31: "Don't include in your income any disability payments (including Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) payments) you receive for injuries incurred as a direct result of a terrorist attack"
findings.why: "Any of your benefits" doesn't say it means only the social security or railroad benefits on SSA-1099/RRB-1099. A filer could answer YES because of a non-SSA disability payment that never enters line 1, and the tool computes those lines correctly.
